look_here_first: Start with WOODY SHRUB + small silver/ash-gray fuzzy leaves (densely matted fine hairs) packed along the branches. Then locate ONE tubular, two-lipped, five-lobed lavender to purple flower emerging from a LEAF AXIL. Count four stamens in two length pairs when flower is accessible. The common name 'Texas sage' is NOT Salvia texana.

project_inclusion.learner_admission_basis: Master Plant Pool row 636, My iNaturalist flora and personal list, 3 source flags; 9 observations (6 wild-tagged, 3 cultivated), Hays Local in tracker.
project_inclusion.range_basis: Native to Texas (native range predominantly South Texas/Trans-Pecos) per UT Austin herbarium and Texas A&M; BONAP/NAPA county distribution needs reconciliation for at least 3 of 24 project counties. Hays-area observations and nursery plantings do not prove historic indigenous range.

morphology_keys.habit: Much-branched evergreen or seasonally semi-evergreen woody shrub to about 2.5 m; gray older bark, no spines; natural shrubs often irregular rather than sheared balls.
morphology_keys.leaves: Small simple entire-margined elliptic to obovate blades, mostly under about 2.5 cm, pale gray from dense soft matted trichomes; foliage often crowded on short shoots and sometimes appears paired though generally described as alternate/clustered; distinguish leaf arrangement on several nodes rather than one tight tuft.
morphology_keys.leaf_hairs: Dense fine soft woolly hairs (tomentum) give ashy silver color; a hand lens and good macro help distinguish hair surface from waxy/glaucous coating.
morphology_keys.flowers: Usually solitary in upper leaf axils; pink-lavender to violet, occasionally white; funnel/bell-shaped tubular corolla, five unequal lobes arranged in two lips, throat may have darker spotting and hairs.
morphology_keys.reproductive: Usually four fertile stamens (two longer, two shorter, didynamous); superior two-carpellate ovary, mature fruit a dry many-seeded capsule splitting by two valves. Clear stamen/calyx/fruit views needed in final photo polish.
morphology_keys.habitat: Limestone/caliche hillsides and dry brushlands, widespread in South Texas and used ornamentally well outside indigenous stands.

comparisons.key_distinctions: True Salvia is Lamiaceae: often strongly four-angled herbaceous stems, opposite leaves, flowers in verticillasters and typically two fertile stamens; cenizo is a woody Scrophulariaceae shrub with densely gray hairy leaves and single axillary tubular flowers with four fertile stamens. Other Leucophyllum/cultivars can have overlapping leaf/flower characters: avoid exact taxon or wild-origin calls from bloom color or foliage brightness alone. Silverleaf nightshade has rotate/starry flowers and may have prickles, not cenizo's tubular bilabiate flower.
